reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: This chapter addresses the structural aspects and limit states for driven pile foundations following the AASHTO (2014) LRFD Bridge Design Specifications. The factored structural resistances for piles are a function of average section yield strength, factors for incision, loading rate, submersion, cross sectional shape, and analysis method for timber piles, resistance factor phi_i for variations in loading condition, materials, and method reliability, and load factor gamma_i to account for uncertainty in the factored service loads. AASHTO (2014) addresses the structural resistance of concrete piles in Article 5, steel piles in Article 6, and timber piles in Article 8.
key_points: Structural resistance must exceed factored loads applied to the pile
AASHTO (2014) LRFD methodology governs structural pile design
Driving stress limits, group layout, preliminary cap design, in-service stress limits, and buckling are addressed
Factored structural resistance depends on yield strength, resistance factors, and load factors
Material-specific provisions: concrete (Article 5), steel (Article 6), timber (Article 8)
sections.applicability: Overview of structural design requirements for all driven pile materials per AASHTO LRFD.

sections.title: Basic Structural Properties of Driven Piles
sections.body: Primary pile materials include steel, concrete, and timber. The properties of these materials significantly affect static nominal structural resistance and nominal driving resistance. Steel piles are produced to meet minimum design yield stress standards, concrete pile resistance depends on elastic modulus and compression strength, and timber pile properties vary by tree species. Section geometry and moment of inertia calculations are essential for evaluating combined axial and flexural loading.
key_points: Steel elastic modulus E_s = 29,000 ksi per AASHTO (2014)
Concrete elastic modulus estimated from compression strength via Eq. 8-1
Timber properties vary by species; Douglas-Fir and Southern Pine most common
Moment of inertia formulas provided for circular, voided circular, and square sections
Section modulus S = I/c used for moment-induced stress calculations
H-pile and pipe pile section properties tabulated in Figures 8-1 through 8-3
sections.applicability: Material and section property fundamentals for all driven pile structural analyses.

sections.title: Material Properties
sections.body: Steel piles are generally produced to meet a minimum design yield stress. Common steel pipe pile grades (ASTM A-252) range from 35 to 80 ksi yield stress, while H-pile grades (A-36 and ASTM A-572) range from 36 to 60 ksi. ASTM A572 now requires new H-pile sections to be produced with a minimum yield stress of 50 ksi, so A-36 grade H-piles are no longer manufactured. For concrete piles, the elastic modulus is estimated from the 28-day compression strength. Timber pile properties including compression stress parallel to grain and elastic modulus are provided for Douglas-Fir, Red Oak, Red Pine, and Southern Pine.
key_points: Steel pipe pile grades: ASTM A-252 Grades 2, 3, and 3 (Mod), Fy = 35 to 80 ksi
Steel H-pile grades: A-36 (Fy=36 ksi), ASTM A-572-50 (Fy=50 ksi), A-572-60 (Fy=60 ksi)
A-36 H-piles no longer manufactured; ASTM A572 requires minimum 50 ksi
Concrete elastic modulus Ec = 1820*sqrt(f'c) assuming 145 pcf unit weight
Timber species: Douglas-Fir (Fco=1.25, Eo=1500 ksi), Southern Pine (Fco=1.20, Eo=1500 ksi)
Red Oak (Fco=1.10, Eo=1250 ksi) and Red Pine (Fco=0.90, Eo=1280 ksi) also used

sections.title: Pile Section Definitions
sections.body: Beyond material properties, the general shape and element dimensions affect modes of structural resistance. The relative thickness of steel limits the magnitude of force that can be transferred to the pile during driving or for structural considerations. Axial compression and flexural resistance are derived from the pile shape. Moment of inertia (I) is computed for various common shapes, and the elastic section modulus (S = I/c) is used to evaluate moment-induced stresses. Sections should be selected from those commonly available from local suppliers.
key_points: Pile shape and dimensions affect axial compression and flexural resistance modes
Moment of inertia formulas provided for solid circular, voided circular, and solid square sections
Elastic section modulus S = I/c for moment stress evaluation
H-pile section properties tabulated in Figure 8-2 (Skyline Steel 2015)
Reference AISC (2011) shape tables for detailed strong and weak axis properties
Select sections from locally available stock to avoid scheduling delays

sections.title: Effective Length and Buckling
sections.body: From a structural view, piles act as columns under axial or moment loads. An effective length is determined using an effective length factor K based on pile end conditions. Buckling is generally a concern when piles extend through water or air, or for liquefaction where confining stress is absent. Research by Bethlehem Steel Corporation (1970) and Coduto et al. (2016) suggests that even the softest soils provide enough lateral support to prevent underground buckling in piles subject to axial loads, especially when a cap provides rotational fixity. A more rigorous approach uses computer software such as LPILE to generate a pile-soil model and evaluate deflection under incremental loads.
key_points: Piles act as columns; effective length factor K depends on end conditions
K values range from 0.65 (fixed-fixed) to 2.0 (free-free) per AASHTO (2014)
Buckling primarily a concern for piles through water, air, liquefiable soils, or very soft soils
Research indicates even soft soils provide adequate lateral support against buckling
Rotationally fixed pile top requires cap connection design per Rollins and Stenlund (2010)
Computer software (LPILE) can evaluate buckling with pile-soil interaction model

sections.title: Structural Considerations and Resistance Factors
sections.body: The limitations on nominal static design stresses for driven piles in various codes represent the static resistance that can be consistently developed with traditional driving equipment and methods. The factored resistance must be greater than factored loads applied to the pile. The recommended AASHTO limits for factored pile design stresses will generally keep driving stresses within recommended limits. Factored loads are covered in Article 3 of the AASHTO Specification (2014) while driving stress limits are presented in the respective pile material sections.
key_points: Factored resistance must exceed factored loads per LRFD methodology
AASHTO factored pile design stress limits keep driving stresses within recommended limits
Factored loads defined in AASHTO Article 3 (load combinations)
Driving stress limits in material-specific AASHTO articles: concrete (5), steel (6), timber (8)
Resistance factors applied to nominal structural resistance per LRFD approach
sections.applicability: Framework for LRFD structural resistance evaluation of driven piles.

sections.title: Depth to Fixity
sections.body: The unbraced length l is defined by AASHTO (2014) as the distance between two braced points that resist buckling or distortion modes. For embedded piles, the unbraced length is considered for scour and pile stickup through air and/or water. For preliminary analysis with lateral loads, the effective length K is taken as the total unsupported length plus an embedded depth to fixity. If a lateral pile analysis with p-y curves has been performed, the depth to fixity concept is unnecessary. The depth to fixity below ground is evaluated based on soil type: for clays using the clay soil modulus Es, and for sands using the rate of increase in soil modulus with depth nh.
key_points: Unbraced length = distance between braced points resisting buckling
Depth to fixity needed for preliminary analysis; not needed if p-y analysis is performed
For clays: df = 1.4*(E*Iw/Es)^0.25, where Es = 0.465*su
For sands: df = 1.8*(E*Iw/nh)^0.2
Table 8-4 provides nh values for loose, medium, and dense sands
Most lateral analysis software includes buckling evaluation features

sections.title: Limiting Slenderness Ratio
sections.body: Piles extending through air or water are unbraced over some length and therefore for axial compression, the slenderness ratio should be checked during design. For non-composite steel piles which are not fully embedded, the slenderness ratio Kl/rs must not exceed 120, where K is the effective length factor, l is the unbraced length plus depth to fixity, and rs is the minimum radius of gyration.
key_points: Slenderness ratio check required for piles with unbraced length through air or water
Limiting slenderness ratio: Kl/rs <= 120 for non-composite steel piles
K = effective length factor from Figure 8-4
l = unbraced length including laterally unsupported length plus df
rs = minimum radius of gyration = sqrt(I/A)

sections.title: Resistance Factors
sections.body: The AASHTO (2014) LRFD approach applies resistance factors to calculated nominal structural resistance. The imposed factored load must be less than or equal to the factored resistance. Factored loads include axial (Pu), moment (Mu), and shear (Vu). Factored resistances are computed as phi*Pn for compression, phi*Mn for flexure, and phi*Vn for shear. AASHTO recommended resistance factors for driving and structural applications are provided in Tables 8-5 and 8-6 respectively. For example, a steel H-pile with good driving conditions and no pile tip needed has phi_c = 0.60 for axial compression, while for combined axial and flexural for undamaged piles phi_c = 0.70.
key_points: LRFD: factored load <= factored resistance (phi * nominal resistance)
Factored axial load: sum(ni*gammai*Qi) = Pu
Factored resistance in compression: Pr = phi_c * Pn
Factored resistance in flexure: Mr = phi_f * Mn
Factored resistance in shear: Vr = phi_v * Vn
Driving resistance factors: steel phi_da=1.0, concrete phi_da=1.0, timber phi_da=1.15
Structural resistance factors vary by material, pile type, and loading condition (Table 8-6)

sections.title: Timber Piles
sections.body: Timber piles are typically round, tapered, and used for modest loading levels. Douglas Fir and Southern Pine are by far the most common types used in the United States. Reference design values in Table 8-7 include compression stress parallel to grain (Fco), flexural strength (Fbo), shear strength (Fvo), and elastic modulus (Eo). The reference values are modified by adjustment factors specific to the loading case and pile properties. The time effect factor C_lambda (Table 8-8) accounts for loading duration: Strength I uses C_lambda=0.8, Strength II and III use 1.0, and Strength IV uses 0.6.
key_points: Timber piles are round, tapered, used for modest loading levels
Douglas Fir and Southern Pine are the predominant species in the US
Reference design values include Fco, Fbo, Fvo, and Eo (Table 8-7)
Time effect factor C_lambda varies by limit state (Table 8-8)
Size reduction factor C_F applied for sections with area > 144 in^2 in flexure
Wet service factor C_M = 1.0 recommended for piles

sections.title: Driving Stresses (Timber)
sections.body: Timber piles should be installed to limit excessive pile stress development that may result in shearing or brooming near the pile top. Additional stresses may develop along the pile as the tapered section decreases near the pile toe. AASHTO (2014) specifications limit maximum compression and tension driving stresses per Equation 8-17, using the driving resistance factor phi_da = 1.15 for timber piles.
key_points: Driving may cause shearing or brooming near pile top
Stress development increases as tapered section decreases near toe
Maximum driving stress: sigma_dr = phi_da * (2.6 * Fco)
Driving resistance factor phi_da = 1.15 for timber piles (Table 8-5)
Fco = reference compression stress parallel to grain (Table 8-7)

sections.title: Structural Resistance (Timber)
sections.body: AASHTO (2014) summarizes axial and flexural resistance limits in Articles 8.6, 8.8, and 8.10. The structural resistance calculations use reference design values from Table 8-7, modified by adjustment factors including the format conversion factor C_KF, wet service factor C_M, size factor C_F, incising factor C_i, and time effect factor C_lambda. The adjustment factors for timber piles are generally set to 1.0 per AASHTO guidance, with the exception of C_KF which converts from ASD to LRFD format and C_lambda for time effects.
key_points: Axial compression resistance: Pr = phi * Pn with phi = 0.9
Flexural resistance: Mr = phi * Mn with phi = 0.85
Format conversion factor C_KF = 2.5/phi converts ASD to LRFD
Wet service factor C_M = 1.0, incising factor C_i = 1.0 for piles
Column stability factor C_p accounts for buckling if insufficient bracing
Combined flexure and axial compression interaction check required (Eq. 8-30)

sections.title: Steel Piles
sections.body: Steel piles can handle higher stresses than concrete or timber during driving, and the stress limit is governed by the steel yield strength. Several grades of steel are routinely produced and higher grades may be specified if warranted. Pile driving does not typically generate sufficiently high tensile stresses to yield steel piles, therefore a stress limit is only required in compression. Steel piles are primarily H-piles or pipe piles, and the structural resistance procedures address axial compression, flexure, combined loading, and shear for both section types.
key_points: Steel piles handle highest driving stresses among pile materials
Driving stress limit governed by yield strength; only compression limit needed
Primary types: H-piles and pipe piles
Structural checks: axial compression, flexure, combined axial/flexure, and shear
Slender element reduction factor Q may apply for local buckling
Both flexural and torsional buckling modes must be checked for H-piles

sections.title: Driving Stresses (Steel)
sections.body: For steel piles, AASHTO (2014) specifications limit nominal compression driving stresses to 0.9 times the yield stress, multiplied by the driving resistance factor phi_da = 1.0. Pile driving does not typically generate sufficient tensile stresses to yield steel piles, so tension driving stress limits are not required.
key_points: Maximum driving stress: sigma_dr = phi_da * (0.9 * Fy)
phi_da = 1.0 for steel piles (Table 8-5)
Compression driving stress only; tension limit not required
Fy = yield stress of steel (Table 8-1 for pipe, Table 8-2 for H-piles)

equations.notes: Compression only. Tension driving stress not required for steel piles.

sections.title: Structural Resistance (Steel)
sections.body: Steel pile structural resistance is evaluated for axial compression (Section 8.5.2.1), flexure (Section 8.5.2.2), combined axial compression and flexure (Section 8.5.2.3), and shear (Section 8.5.2.4). The step-by-step procedures follow AASHTO (2014) Articles 6.9.4 and 6.12.2.2. For axial compression, the nominal resistance considers both yield and buckling failure modes. For flexure, the procedure differs for H-sections (slenderness-based) and pipe piles (D/t ratio-based). The example calculations in Section 8.5.3 demonstrate the complete procedure for an HP14x117 pile.
key_points: Factored axial resistance: Pr = phi_c * Pn (Eq. 8-34)
Factored flexural resistance: Mr = phi_f * Mn (Eq. 8-45)
Nominal axial resistance considers yield (Po) and elastic buckling (Pe)
If Pe/Po >= 0.44: Pn = Po * 0.658^(Po/Pe) (inelastic buckling)
If Pe/Po < 0.44: Pn = 0.877 * Pe (elastic buckling)
H-pile flexure: slenderness ratio determines compact, non-compact, or slender
Pipe pile flexure: D/t ratio determines plastic moment or local buckling controls
Combined checks differ for Pu/Pr < 0.2 vs >= 0.2

sections.title: Example Calculations for H Pile Structural Resistance
sections.body: A worked example is provided for an HP 14x117 pile supporting an integral abutment with Fy = 50 ksi, Est = 29,000 ksi, rs = 3.59 inches, and unbraced length l = 120 inches due to scour. With K = 1.2 and good driving conditions, the calculations demonstrate: (1) non-slender element check via kc and Eq. 8-36 giving Q = 1.0, (2) equivalent yield resistance Po = 1720 kips, (3) elastic critical buckling Pe = 6120 kips, (4) nominal axial resistance Pn = 1529 kips via Eq. 8-43, (5) factored axial resistance Pr = 917 kips (phi_c=0.60), (6) flange slenderness lambda_f = 9.25 compared to lambda_pf = 9.25 and lambda_rf = 19.98, (7) nominal flexural resistance Mn = 4555 kip-in via Eq. 8-51, (8) factored flexural resistance Mr = 4555 kip-in (phi_f=1.0), and (9) factored shear resistance Vr = 332 kips.
key_points: Unbraced length l=120 in (scour), K=1.2 (fixed rotation/free translation at head)
kc = 0.76 (bounded), non-slender element (Q=1.0)
Po = 1720 kips, Pe = 6120 kips, Pe/Po = 3.56 >= 0.44
Pn = 1529 kips (inelastic buckling), Pr = 917 kips (phi_c=0.60)

sections.title: Concrete Piles
sections.body: Concrete is strong in compression while tensile strength is mainly derived from reinforcing steel and prestressed longitudinal rebar. The additional tensile strength from prestressing allows for larger tensile stresses and is featured in nearly all concrete piles manufactured today. Unlike timber and steel piles, concrete piles are susceptible to damage in both compression and tension under normal driving conditions. Pile cushions are employed to slow the impact velocity and reduce dynamic forces during driving.
key_points: Concrete strong in compression; tensile strength from reinforcing/prestressing steel
Nearly all concrete piles manufactured today are prestressed
Susceptible to damage in both compression and tension during driving
Pile cushions used to reduce dynamic forces during driving
Driving stresses applied to gross concrete area
FB-Pier software used for prestressed section analysis with moment interaction diagrams
sections.applicability: Overview of structural design considerations for concrete driven piles.

sections.title: Driving Stresses (Concrete)
sections.body: AASHTO (2014) specifications limit nominal driving stresses for concrete piles in both compression and tension. Driving stress limits are applied to the gross concrete area. In severe corrosive environments, the nominal tension stress is limited to the effective prestress after losses. The resistance factor during driving phi_da = 1.0 for concrete piles.
key_points: Compression driving stress: sigma_dr = phi_da * (0.85*f'c - f_pe)
Tension driving stress: sigma_dr = phi_da * (0.095*sqrt(f'c) + f_pe)
phi_da = 1.0 for concrete piles (Table 8-5)
f_pe = effective prestressing stress, typically 0.5 to 1.0 ksi for highway piles
f_pe must be less than f'c

variables.phi_da: resistance factor during driving (1.0 for concrete, Table 8-5)

equations.notes: f_pe typically 0.5 to 1.0 ksi for highway projects.

sections.title: Structural Resistance (Concrete)
sections.body: The structural resistance of concrete piles is evaluated for axial compression and biaxial flexure. For axial compression, the nominal resistance accounts for the concrete strength, reinforcing steel, and prestressing steel. Reduction factors of 0.85 (spiral reinforcement) or 0.80 (tie reinforcement) are applied to account for unintended eccentricity. Biaxial flexure resistance is evaluated using moment interaction diagrams, typically generated using FB-Pier software. The analysis uses stress-strain relationships for concrete and prestressing steel to construct a three-dimensional failure surface.
key_points: Factored axial resistance: Pr = phi_c * Pn (Eq. 8-64)
Spiral reinforcement: Pn = 0.85[0.85*f'c*(Ag-Astr-Aps) + Fyr*Astr - Aps*(fpe - Est*ecu)]
Tie reinforcement: factor is 0.80 instead of 0.85
Biaxial flexure: Mr = phi_f * Mn (Eq. 8-67)
Interaction check for Pu >= 0.10*phi*f'c*Ag: 1/Prxy = 1/Prx + 1/Pry - 1/(phi*Po)
Interaction check for Pu < 0.10*phi*f'c*Ag: Mux/Mrx + Muy/Mry <= 1.0
FB-Pier generates 3D failure surface from stacked interaction diagrams
Resistance factors: tension controlled RC phi_c=0.90, PS phi_c=1.00, compression PS phi_c=0.75

Nominal axial compression resistance for concrete piles with spiral reinforcement

sections.title: Composite Piles
sections.body: Composite piles for structural applications are defined as concrete filled steel pipe piles. Guidance for other composite pile types such as concrete piles with H-pile stingers is not provided in AASHTO (2014). For composite sections, driving stresses follow the non-composite steel section procedures (Section 8.5.1). The structural resistance is evaluated using a normalized column slenderness factor and composite section properties. AASHTO (2014) evaluation methods require: (1) steel area at least 4% of total area, (2) concrete compression strength between 3.0 and 8.0 ksi, and (3) reinforcing steel yield strength not exceeding 60.0 ksi.
key_points: Composite piles = concrete filled steel pipe piles per AASHTO (2014)
Driving stresses evaluated as non-composite steel section (Section 8.5.1)
Steel area must be at least 4% of total cross-sectional area
Concrete f'c must be between 3.0 and 8.0 ksi
Reinforcing steel yield strength cannot exceed 60.0 ksi
Nominal resistance uses normalized column slenderness factor lambda
If lambda <= 2.25: Pn = 0.66^lambda * Fe * Ast
If lambda > 2.25: Pn = 0.88 * Fe * Ast / lambda

sections.title: Layout of Pile Groups
sections.body: A group of piles is typically required to support large structural loads. An initial group layout must be determined to perform in-service stress checks. Pile group layouts can be determined using computer software such as GROUP or FB-Pier which utilize soil-structure interaction (t-z and p-y curves) to distribute loads and deflections. Alternatively, a hand calculation using the Rigid Cap Method may be performed. The procedure involves estimating the number of piles required, generating a trial configuration, and checking the maximum single pile factored axial load against the factored structural resistance.
key_points: Number of piles estimated by dividing factored axial load by single pile resistance, rounded up ~15%
Minimum center-to-center spacing: 2.5 feet or 2.5 pile diameters per AASHTO, 3.0 diameters recommended
Rigid Cap Method used for hand calculation of pile forces (Eq. 8-79)
Maximum single pile load must not exceed factored structural resistance
Software (GROUP, FB-Pier) uses t-z and p-y curves for refined analysis
If moments in one direction are larger, unsymmetrical cap layout may be desirable
Critical load combination must be checked, not just the largest axial load

sections.title: Preliminary Design of Pile Bent and Group Caps
sections.body: This section provides guidelines for developing a preliminary size of a pile cap for cost estimating purposes. The LRFD structural design of a concrete pile bent cap is similar to a concrete pier cap. Key design considerations include pile embedment into the cap, structural design depth, pile concrete cover requirements, pile misalignment tolerance, concrete pile anchorage, and minimum pile spacing. The procedure covers estimating cap thickness, determining effective shear depth, checking punching (two-way) shear around columns and individual piles, checking one-way beam shear, and verifying cap flexural resistance.
key_points: Cap thickness estimated as t_cap = Pui/12 + 30 (inches)
Effective shear depth dv = max(0.9*ds, 0.72*h)
Minimum pile embedment: 12 inches after damaged material removal, or 6 inches with embedded bars/strands
Minimum center-to-center spacing: 30 inches or 2.5 pile diameters
Minimum edge of cap to side of pile: 9 inches
Two-way (punching) shear checked around column and individual/paired piles
One-way beam shear checked at critical sections from column face and pile face
Cap flexural resistance: Mu = sum(Rr*(x,y)) <= phi*Mn
Cap moment resistance for preliminary design using d-a/2 approximation

sections.title: Cap Considerations for Large Pile Sizes
sections.body: For Large Diameter Open-Ended Piles (LDOEPs), the general analysis steps from the preceding section should be followed. No strict guidance is available for minimum spacing and embedment into the pier cap for large pile sizes, as most state agencies do not currently have standard plans for these pile sizes. Case studies presented in Brown and Thompson (2014) show pile tops embedded approximately 3 feet into the pier cap for LDOEPs. Pile spacing considerations should reflect drilled shaft guidelines, with a minimum spacing on the order of 3 pile diameters (center to center), consistent with typical drilled shaft group layouts.
key_points: LDOEPs: follow general pile cap design steps
No strict guidance for LDOEP minimum spacing and embedment
Pile tops embedded approximately 3 feet into pier cap for LDOEPs
Minimum spacing: approximately 3 pile diameters (center to center)
Spacing consistent with drilled shaft group layout guidelines (Brown et al. 2010)
